claims.text: A Mo-Nb-Ta-W-type refractory high-entropy alloy has inherent high-temperature resistance.
A Mo-Nb-Ta-W-type refractory high-entropy alloy has inherent irradiation resistance.
The baseline alloy has limited mechanical performance under extreme conditions.
Yttrium and zirconium are low-activation alloying additions suitable for this application.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% each of yttrium and zirconium will promote in situ nanometric precipitate formation.
The resulting precipitates will include complex Y-Zr oxides or related phases.
The precipitates will form a fine, stable dispersion at grain boundaries and within grains.
The nano-precipitates will impede dislocation motion.
The nano-precipitates will pin irradiation-generated defect clusters and impede defect migration.
Impeded dislocation and defect mobility will enhance the alloy's mechanical strength.
Precipitate stability will preserve the alloy's thermal resistance.
Precipitate stability will preserve the alloy's irradiation resistance.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Y-Zr-modified alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Y-Zr-modified alloy will have enhanced ductility.
The mechanical improvements will occur without a significant loss of high-temperature stability.
The mechanical improvements will occur without a significant loss of irradiation stability.
The beneficial effects are expected between approximately 800°C and 1200°C under simulated irradiation.
Additions substantially above 1–2 at.% may cause unwanted phase changes or precipitate coarsening.
Temperatures far outside 800°C–1200°C or extreme irradiation flux may cause unwanted phase changes or precipitate coarsening.
Unwanted phase changes or precipitate coarsening would negate the proposed mechanical improvements.
